lessons.title: Properties of transition metals
lessons.summary: Compare the transition metals with the group 1 metals, and learn the four special properties that make transition metals so useful: variable ion charges, coloured compounds, catalytic behaviour and strength.
objectives: I can locate the transition metals on the periodic table.
I can compare the physical and chemical properties of transition metals with those of group 1 metals.
I can describe the typical properties of transition metals: ions with different charges, coloured compounds and use as catalysts.
I can give examples of transition metals used as catalysts and explain why this is useful.

activities.title: Where are the transition metals?
activities.content:
## The central block

Between group 2 and group 3 of the periodic table sits a wide block of elements: the **transition metals**. The row you will meet most often runs from **titanium (Ti)** across to **copper (Cu)** and includes familiar metals such as **chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt and nickel**.

These are the metals that engineers, builders and jewellers reach for. Iron makes steel for bridges and cars, copper carries electricity through cables, and nickel and chromium give stainless steel its shine.

Like all metals, transition metals:

- conduct heat and electricity
- are shiny when freshly cut
- are malleable (can be hammered into shape) and ductile (drawn into wires)

But compared with the metals in **group 1** (lithium, sodium, potassium), transition metals behave very differently. Learning to spell out these differences is the main job of this lesson. Keep the alkali metals in mind as your comparison point throughout.

activities.title: Transition metals versus group 1
activities.content:
## Compare and contrast

| Property | Group 1 metals | Transition metals |
|---|---|---|
| Melting point | low (potassium melts at 63 °C) | high (iron melts at 1538 °C) |
| Density | low; Li, Na, K float on water | high; iron is about 8 times denser than water |
| Hardness | soft, cut with a knife | hard and strong |
| Reaction with water | rapid, fizzing, forms hydroxide + hydrogen | slow or none at room temperature |
| Reaction with oxygen | tarnish within seconds in air | react slowly (iron rusts over weeks) |
| Reaction with halogens | vigorous | much less vigorous |
| Ion charge | always +1 | can be different (Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺) |
| Colour of compounds | white or colourless | usually coloured |

The simple summary: transition metals are **stronger, denser, higher-melting and far less reactive** than group 1 metals.

The low reactivity matters. Sodium would be useless for a saucepan because it would react with the water in your soup; iron and copper are stable enough to last for years.

question.text: Which of these statements correctly compare transition metals with group 1 metals? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Think about iron and sodium: which would you rather build a bridge from?
question.explanation: Transition metals have higher melting points and are less reactive with water. They are denser (not less dense) and are harder, not softer.

options.text: Transition metals have higher melting points
Transition metals react less vigorously with water

options.feedback: Group 1 metals float on water; transition metals sink.
Sodium can be cut with a knife; iron cannot.

activities.title: Ions with different charges
activities.content:
## Variable charges

A sodium atom always forms **Na⁺**. It has one outer electron, loses it, and that is the end of the story.

Transition metals are different. The same element can form **ions with more than one charge**, depending on the reaction. For example:

- iron forms **Fe²⁺** (in iron(II) chloride, FeCl₂) and **Fe³⁺** (in iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃)
- copper forms **Cu⁺** (in copper(I) oxide, Cu₂O) and **Cu²⁺** (in copper(II) oxide, CuO)
- chromium forms Cr²⁺, Cr³⁺ and even Cr⁶⁺ in some compounds

The Roman numeral in the name tells you the charge on the metal ion. This is why chemists write **iron(III) oxide** rather than just "iron oxide": without the numeral you cannot tell whether the formula is FeO or Fe₂O₃.

When you write a formula, use the charge to balance the compound. Fe³⁺ needs three Cl⁻ ions to cancel its charge, so iron(III) chloride is **FeCl₃**.

activities.title: Worked example: naming and formulae
activities.content:
**Write the formula of copper(II) sulfate, and name the compound CuCl.**

*Copper(II) sulfate:* the (II) tells us the copper ion is **Cu²⁺**. The sulfate ion is **SO₄²⁻**. The charges are equal and opposite, so one of each is needed: **CuSO₄**.

*CuCl:* the chloride ion is Cl⁻, and there is only one of it, so the copper ion must be Cu⁺ to make the compound neutral. The name is **copper(I) chloride**.

**Now try manganese(IV) oxide.** Mn⁴⁺ needs two O²⁻ ions (2 × −2 = −4) to balance: **MnO₂**.

question.text: Complete the sentences about iron compounds.

metadata.blanksText: In FeO the iron ion has a charge of ___, so the compound is named iron(II) oxide. In Fe₂O₃ the iron ion has a charge of ___, so the compound is named iron(III) oxide.

question.hint: Each oxide ion is 2−. Balance the total positive charge against the total negative charge.
question.explanation: FeO: one O²⁻ balances one Fe²⁺ (+2). Fe₂O₃: three O²⁻ give −6, so two iron ions must total +6, i.e. Fe³⁺ each (+3).

activities.title: Coloured compounds
activities.content:
## A splash of colour

Compounds of group 1 metals are almost always **white solids** that dissolve to give **colourless solutions**. Sodium chloride, potassium nitrate and lithium carbonate all look the same: white.

Transition metal compounds are usually **coloured**, and the colour depends on both the metal and the charge on its ion:

| Ion | Typical colour in solution |
|---|---|
| Cu²⁺ | blue |
| Fe²⁺ | pale green |
| Fe³⁺ | orange-brown |
| Ni²⁺ | green |
| MnO₄⁻ (manganate(VII)) | deep purple |

This is why copper sulfate crystals are blue, rust (iron(III) oxide) is orange-brown, and the pigments in many paints and glazes contain transition metals. Cobalt compounds give blue glass its colour; chromium gives rubies their red.

Colour is also a handy clue in the lab. If you see a coloured solution or precipitate, a transition metal is probably involved. The later analysis topic uses hydroxide precipitates (blue for copper, green for iron(II), brown for iron(III)) to identify these ions.

question.text: A student has two white powders and one blue powder. Which powder is most likely to be a transition metal compound?
question.hint: Which group's compounds are usually coloured?
question.explanation: Transition metal compounds are usually coloured; group 1 compounds are typically white. The blue powder is most likely a transition metal compound such as copper sulfate.

options.feedback: White compounds are typical of group 1 metals.

activities.title: Transition metals as catalysts
activities.content:
## Speeding up reactions

A **catalyst** speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up, so a small amount can be used over and over. Many transition metals and their compounds are excellent catalysts, and industry depends on them:

- **Iron** catalyses the **Haber process**, which makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen for fertilisers.
- **Nickel** catalyses the **hydrogenation** of vegetable oils to make solid spreads such as margarine.
- **Vanadium(V) oxide** (V₂O₅) catalyses a key step in making **sulfuric acid**.
- **Platinum, palladium and rhodium** in a car's **catalytic converter** turn harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones.
- **Manganese(IV) oxide** speeds up the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen in the school lab.

Why are they good at it? Transition metals can form ions with different charges, so they can accept and give back electrons easily during a reaction, offering the reacting molecules an easier route.

Catalysts save money and energy: reactions run faster at lower temperatures, and the catalyst is not consumed.

activities.title: Worked example: choosing a catalyst
activities.content:
**A factory makes ammonia. Which transition metal catalyst should it use, and why does using a catalyst make the process cheaper?**

*Catalyst:* **iron**, which is used in the Haber process.

*Why cheaper:* the reaction reaches a useful rate at a **lower temperature**, so less fuel is burned to heat the reactors. The iron is **not used up**, so it does not need constant replacing. Faster reactions mean more product made per day from the same equipment.

**Extra point for a higher grade:** iron is also chosen because it is cheap and plentiful compared with metals such as platinum. A catalyst that costs more than the product it helps make would be a poor choice.

question.text: Match each transition metal catalyst to the process it is used in.
question.explanation: Iron catalyses the Haber process (ammonia); nickel catalyses hydrogenation of vegetable oils; vanadium(V) oxide is used in making sulfuric acid.

pairs.right: Making ammonia in the Haber process

question.text: True or false: a transition metal catalyst is used up during the reaction it speeds up, so it must be replaced after each batch.
question.hint: What is the definition of a catalyst?
question.explanation: False. A catalyst is not used up by the reaction, which is one reason catalysts are so economical.

question.text:
Copper is a transition metal. Sodium is a group 1 metal.

(a) Give two physical properties of copper that make it more suitable than sodium for making water pipes. (2 marks)

(b) Copper forms two oxides, Cu₂O and CuO. Explain what this tells you about copper ions. (2 marks)
question.hint: For (a), think about strength and how each metal behaves near water. For (b), work out the charge on copper in each oxide.
question.explanation: (a) Copper is hard/strong and does not react with water (sodium is soft and reacts violently with water). Copper also has a high melting point. (b) In Cu₂O copper is Cu⁺; in CuO it is Cu²⁺. So copper can form ions with different charges, which is a typical transition metal property.

markScheme.criterion: Copper is hard / strong / has a high melting point
Copper does not react with water / is unreactive, whereas sodium reacts with water
Identifies the ions as Cu+ (in Cu2O) and Cu2+ (in CuO)
Copper forms ions with different charges

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Transition metals sit in the **central block** of the periodic table (e.g. Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu).
- Compared with group 1 metals they are **harder, denser, higher-melting and much less reactive** with water, oxygen and halogens.
- They form **ions with different charges** (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺); Roman numerals in names show the charge.
- Their compounds are usually **coloured** (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ orange-brown).
- Many are **catalysts**: iron (Haber process), nickel (hydrogenating oils), vanadium(V) oxide (sulfuric acid).

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these elements is a transition metal?
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for the element from the central block of the table.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Nickel is a transition metal. Sodium and calcium are in groups 1 and 2; sulfur is a non-metal.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: transition metals generally have higher densities than group 1 metals.
practiceQuestions.hint: Sodium floats on water; does iron?
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Iron, copper and nickel are all much denser than water, whereas lithium, sodium and potassium float.

metadata.blanksText: The catalyst used in the Haber process to make ammonia is ___, and the catalyst used to hydrogenate vegetable oils is ___.

practiceQuestions.hint: One is the main metal in steel; the other is used in coins.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Iron catalyses the Haber process; nickel is used to hydrogenate oils.

practiceQuestions.text: In the compound CrCl₃, what is the charge on the chromium ion? Give your answer as a number (e.g. 2 for 2+).
practiceQuestions.hint: Each chloride ion has a charge of 1−. The compound is neutral overall.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Three Cl⁻ ions give −3, so the chromium ion must be Cr³⁺, a charge of +3.

practiceQuestions.text: Which colour would you expect a solution containing copper(II) ions to be?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cu²⁺ ions give a blue solution.

options.feedback: Colourless solutions are typical of group 1 compounds.

practiceQuestions.text: Arrange these metals from most reactive with water to least reactive.
practiceQuestions.hint: Group 1 metals are far more reactive than transition metals; reactivity in group 1 increases down the group.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Potassium (group 1, lower down) is most reactive, then lithium (group 1, top), then iron (a transition metal, reacts only slowly), then copper (does not react with water).

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why using a catalyst makes an industrial process cheaper to run.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about temperature and about whether the catalyst needs replacing.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A catalyst lets the reaction happen quickly at a lower temperature, saving energy costs. It is not used up, so it does not need to be continually replaced.

markScheme.criterion: Reaction can run at a lower temperature / uses less energy
Catalyst is not used up / can be reused

practiceQuestions.text: Which of the following are typical properties of transition metals? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Two of the four are typical of group 1 metals instead.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Transition metals form coloured compounds and act as catalysts. Forming only +1 ions and reacting vigorously with cold water are group 1 properties.

options.feedback: Transition metals can form ions with different charges.

practiceQuestions.text: A student is given two unlabelled metal samples. One is potassium and one is manganese. Describe two tests or observations the student could use to tell which sample is the transition metal, and state the expected result for each.
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare hardness, density, or the reaction with water.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Hardness: manganese is hard, potassium can be cut with a knife. Density: potassium floats on water, manganese sinks. Reaction with water: potassium fizzes violently and may ignite; manganese reacts very slowly. Any two tests with correct results earn the marks; a third mark is for correctly identifying manganese as the transition metal from the results.

markScheme.criterion: A valid test with correct result, e.g. cut with a knife: potassium is soft, manganese is hard
A second valid test with correct result, e.g. add to water: potassium fizzes/reacts violently, manganese does not; or density: potassium floats, manganese sinks
Concludes that the harder / denser / less reactive sample is manganese, the transition metal

practiceQuestions.text: What is the correct name of the compound with the formula FeCl₂?
practiceQuestions.hint: Two Cl⁻ ions must be balanced by the charge on one iron ion.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Two chloride ions give −2, so the iron ion is Fe²⁺ and the compound is iron(II) chloride.

options.feedback: Iron(III) chloride would need three chloride ions: FeCl₃.

practiceQuestions.text: Nickel is a transition metal and sodium is a group 1 metal. Which of these statements are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Sodium is soft, light and fizzes on water. Nickel is used in coins.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sodium reacts vigorously with water while nickel hardly reacts at all, and nickel is much harder than sodium. Nickel is denser than sodium (sodium floats on water) and has a far higher melting point, so the last two statements are wrong.

options.text: Sodium reacts more vigorously with water than nickel does

options.feedback: Sodium floats on water; nickel is far denser.

options.text: Nickel melts at a lower temperature than sodium
options.feedback: Transition metals have much higher melting points than group 1 metals.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about manganese compounds.

metadata.blanksText: In MnO the manganese ion has a charge of ___, so the compound is named manganese(II) oxide. In MnO₂ the manganese ion has a charge of ___, so the compound is named manganese(IV) oxide.

practiceQuestions.hint: Every oxide ion is 2−. The total positive charge must cancel the total negative charge in each formula.
practiceQuestions.explanation: MnO: one O²⁻ (−2) is balanced by one Mn²⁺ (+2). MnO₂: two O²⁻ give −4, so the single manganese ion must be +4 (Mn⁴⁺).

practiceQuestions.text: A student is given three solutions: one is colourless, one is pale green and one is pink. Which of the solutions are most likely to contain transition metal ions?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the appearance of a copper sulfate solution with a sodium chloride solution.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Transition metal ions usually give coloured solutions, whereas group 1 compounds give colourless solutions. The green and pink solutions are most likely to contain transition metal ions (for example iron(II) or manganese(II)).

options.text: The pale green and the pink solutions

options.feedback: Colourless solutions are typical of group 1 compounds, not transition metal compounds.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each industrial process to the transition metal catalyst it uses.
practiceQuestions.hint: Iron for ammonia, nickel for hardening oils, vanadium(V) oxide for sulfuric acid.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Haber process (nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia) uses an iron catalyst. Hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make solid spreads uses nickel. The oxidation of sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide in sulfuric acid manufacture uses vanadium(V) oxide.

pairs.left: Combining nitrogen and hydrogen to make ammonia
Turning liquid vegetable oil into a solid spread
Converting sulfur dioxide to sulfur trioxide when making sulfuric acid

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: a transition metal catalyst can be recovered unchanged at the end of a reaction, so the same small amount can be used again and again.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what happens to a catalyst during the reaction it speeds up.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up, so it is chemically unchanged at the end and can be reused many times.

practiceQuestions.text:
Iron is a transition metal. Potassium is a group 1 metal.

(a) Give two physical properties of iron that make it more suitable than potassium for building a bridge. (2 marks)

(b) Cobalt, another transition metal, forms two chlorides, CoCl₂ and CoCl₃. Explain what this tells you about cobalt ions. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (a), think about strength and about what happens when each metal gets wet. For (b), each chloride ion is 1−; work out the charge on cobalt in each compound.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Iron is hard and strong with a high melting point, and it does not react violently with water; potassium is soft and reacts violently with water. (b) In CoCl₂ cobalt is Co²⁺ and in CoCl₃ it is Co³⁺, so cobalt can form ions with different charges, which is typical of transition metals.

markScheme.criterion: Iron is hard / strong / has a high melting point / is dense
Iron does not react vigorously with water / is much less reactive, whereas potassium reacts violently with water
Identifies the ions as Co2+ (in CoCl2) and Co3+ (in CoCl3)
Cobalt forms ions with different charges
